doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: Childhood in Ohio and first music
title: First musical influences: Hungarian music, swing, country and pop
summary: He describes the Hungarian, swing, WWVA country and pop music around him, and his view that jazz is American rather than black music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: That’s true. So what was the first sort of jazz-related music that caught your ear?

Well this is very interesting. If you’re sensitive to music, as I was and am and hope to be for many more years, in that environment in Ohio there, in the 30s, there was no T.V. of course, there was radio and records. I was exposed to this Hungarian music, you know, which swings you know. Gunter Schuller says you know, that jazz music swings. Jazz is the only one — no, no. Hungarian music, you know, even Romanians even, I mean talk about swing. Anyhow —
Does it have the, doing the off-beats two and four?
But it has a groove to it.

It’s just, you hear it. There’s nothing but rhythm going on. I still have some Romanian LPs you know. It’s outasight. It’s a sense of rhythm and you know like odd tempos in seven and five and you know. Well so anyhow, I was exposed to this Hungarian music. And then I was exposed to the swing era, you know swing music, the big bands you know, that business [scats] sophisticated swing you know. I have a vivid memory of walking through a carnival kind of thing, an outdoor thing, with my mother, late at night.

Maybe we were walking to go home or something, I don’t know how. And over the P.A. system came that. And I liked that, and I said yeah. Years later when I heard it I said ooh I know that. So I was exposed to swing, I was exposed to Hungarian music, and then in that area there was a station, WWVA, and it had the equivalent of Grand Ole Opry. And on Saturday a midnight jamboree or something you know. And they had country players and fiddles and banjos and stuff. And so I had that influence. And so that was country- western. And then of course the Bing Crosby, the pop. Not swing but the pop tunes.
Yeah, the “Pennies From Heaven” type of songs.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. So it was all around me, and I wasn’t necessarily in the cradle of the blues or anything like that. But that’s a funny one. I mean you’ll hear young black guys, I have my own ideas about the origin of jazz, I don’t think it’s black. It’s not a black music, it’s an American music. There was always white and Irishmen and Italians and stuff. And if you’re black and you want to be proud about your black rhythm, that’s marvelous, that’s great, some of the greatest were you know. Joe Oliver, Louis Armstrong, Johnny Dodds. So but anyhow what was I saying? Oh so the midnight jamboree, and all that kind of music, and as a matter of fact my kid singing I continued with that, and they had an amateur contest on WWVA. And really, and I went to it, they had an audition at the amateur contest. And I go down with my mother and, you know we have no music or anything like that, and it was like something from “Our Gang.”
